docs.text: Contributing How this repository is developed and tested — for people changing the code, not using the app. Coding workflow Agent orchestration — bring your own harness (PLANNED, not built) This does not exist yet. The design: a task is a triple — goal, tier, harness preference, due at, blocked by, outcome — and any harness can drain the queue: Claude Code, Codex, a local Ollama script, or a human in the review queue. The graph becomes the orchestration config, so the queue outlives whichever agent CLI is fashionable this quarter, and a harness that hits a usage limit hands its task back rather than stalling it forever. Agents ask the graph, not you When an agent needs a decision it cannot make, it does not stop and wait for you. It emits the question AS A PARTIAL FACT into the graph — subject and predicate known, object '?', plus a note on what the question blocks — and moves to the next unblocked task. You answer whenever you like, in the review queue. The answer flows back and the waiting work resumes. Check your work against the plan (git analysis) The graph knows what you INTENDED. Git knows what you DID. Git analysis compares them: kb check plan tells you whether the work you are about to do matches something planned; kb git diff triples finds which graph entities your diff actually touched; kb alignment score gives a 0 1 score across four dimensions (coverage, status alignment, dependency respect, scope discipline). Commits that match no planned work are flagged as unplanned — not blocked, but not invisible either. CI/CD graph watch — the plan reviews your PR On every push and pull request, CI compares the code changes against the plan in the graph and posts an alignment report as a PR comment: score, discrepancies, drift warnings, and a KB snapshot artifact. Drift is surfaced where the review already happens, rather than in a dashboard nobody opens. Coding workflow Reckons.AI turns a codebase into a graph you can interrogate, and then keeps the code and the plan honest with each other. The plan lives in the graph; code is checked against it; agents propose, humans decide. This page is generated from that same graph, so it cannot claim a capability the graph does not have. Compared with the tools you already use A developer keeping track of a codebase today typically runs three or four separate things: a coding agent that reads the repository, something that maps or searches the code, something that remembers across sessions, and a documentation site. Each is good at its job. The claim here is not that Reckons.AI beats any of them at that job — it does not — but that the four are the same store viewed four ways, and keeping them separate is what makes each of them lose the others' work. Consistency comes from your context, not from a better model The facts that did the work in that session were not general knowledge, and no model would have produced them from training. 'Granularity breeds rubber stamping — a review list that is too fine trains the human to accept all.' 'Cleaning is itself damaging; an automated tidy up that drops a fact you needed is worse than the mess.' 'Spend attention on disagreement, not agreement.' 'Unclassified fails toward the human.' These are one person's judgments, formed on this project, written down once. Because they were in the graph, they constrained work months later — an accept all control shipped WITH outlier highlighting rather than without it, because the graph objected. Feed an agent the graph, not the repo kb compress selects the relevant subgraph for a question and serializes it compactly, so an agent gets grounded context instead of a directory listing. Ingest a repository into a graph Point Reckons.AI at a repository and it builds a Codebase graph: modules, their source files (kpred:has file), and the relationships between them. The result is queryable — 'which module owns this file', 'what does this depend on' — instead of grep and hope. One report that grows, instead of twenty that interrupt Agents append findings — bug found, claim falsified, shipped, decision needed — to a single dated digest while you are away, and each finding is also written into the graph as a pending fact on the entity it concerns. You come back to one accumulating page, not a scrollback to reconstruct. One session, five features not rebuilt Five requests arrived across a single session on 2026 07 19, each framed as new work — and every one of them had already been decided months earlier. The agent had no memory of those sessions; the graph did: (1) 'summarize a node and its relations' was the unbuilt remainder of F65 entity sets, F96 quick graph settings and the graph legibility condensation idea; (2) 'group review triples and accept a set' was loop job grouping, which already specified batch accept with outlier highlighting — only the topical relevance axis was genuinely new; (3) 'graphs need HNSW style jumps to sub graphs' met hierarchy nav (layers within a graph) and KBLeap (jumps between graphs), narrowing the work to the one missing middle rung; (4) 'find the most relevant graph for this ingest' met routeQuestion(), already built and tested, needing only a generalized input; (5) the AI council merge met loop subagent graphs, which had already established that a sub agent returns a graph and that merging graphs is the product. Task scheduling in the graph (PLANNED, not built) This does not exist yet. Tasks, schedules and outcomes as graph facts, drained by whichever runner is available — the in app worker on any device, an optional desktop process, or the MCP server when an agent is already connected. The local agent tier — a first pass that never touches your source A local model (via Ollama, on your own hardware) reviews a diff, drafts a missing description, or reads for staleness — always inside a scripted harness: ground it in the graph, constrain the prompt, validate the output, emit a PROPOSAL. It writes to the review queue. It never writes to source, and it never writes to the graph. The saving is not compression — it is the feature you did not build twice The usual pitch for a knowledge graph in front of a coding agent is token compression: feed a dense subgraph instead of re reading the repo. That saving is real but modest. The larger one is structural — an agent that can query what you already decided proposes an EXTENSION to an existing feature instead of a new feature under a slightly different name. A duplicate feature is not a one off cost: you pay to build it, then pay forever to maintain two things that should have been one, and the second one drifts from the first the first time either is tuned. The script tier — checks that cannot hallucinate Deterministic checks that run on every push and cost nothing: graph invariants (dead file links, invalid statuses, duplicate IDs, dangling dependencies); evidence for status claims (a feature marked shipped must link a test or declare that it has none — you may ship untested code, but not silently); prompt/safety preamble drift; production build verification; and a license gate on every third party dependency we study. Work tiering — stop paying frontier prices for rules Every recurring task is routed to the cheapest tier that can do it correctly. SCRIPT: the answer is checkable by a rule ('does this path exist', 'is this status in the enum') — deterministic code, zero tokens, zero hallucination, runs in CI. LOCAL AGENT: the answer is judgment over language and being wrong is cheap, because the output is a proposal a human gates — a local model inside a scripted harness that grounds it, validates its output, and emits a reviewable proposal. FRONTIER: cross file architectural reasoning, deciding process, and code that lands. Testing Graph Management Page The /kb page showing the graph registry, predicate manager, and workspace controls. Ingest Page The /ingest page with text, URL, file, and graph import tabs. Verified for correct tab rendering and input field visibility. Main Page (Empty graph) The graph view with an empty knowledge graph. Should show the empty state message and Shelly greeting, not a blank screen. Main Page (Mobile) Main graph view on mobile viewport (375x812). NavBar collapses to hamburger, graph fills screen, touch targets are 44px minimum. Main Page (Tablet) Main graph view on tablet viewport (768x1024). Intermediate layout between mobile and desktop. Page Screenshots Baseline visual regression screenshots for each major page. These are not stories but single page captures used for pixel analysis and DOM overlap detection. Reckons.AI Graph Review — Goal & Workflow The Reckons.AI Graph Review is an offline, exhaustive audit of the whole app treated as a graph: every button is clicked, every screen is visually checked, and every finding is tied back to the graph for human review. It runs locally and Opus reviewed — no cloud dependency — and scores against the Web/Mobile UI UX rubric. The goal Catch the failures a "click everything, flag crashes" pass misses — silent no ops (a control that fires, throws nothing, and does nothing) and stale cache regressions — while producing a reviewable, graph native record rather than a throwaway log. Workflow overview 1. Enumerate — collect every interactive element on every route (buttons, tabs, leap badges, sheets). 2. Act and assert a delta — click each, then check that something observable actually changed (URL, node count, graph id, open panels, title, visible text). This is what catches silent no ops. 3. Visual check — pixel, DOM overlap and touch target checks run locally; a local VLM scores each screenshot against the rubric. 4. Persistent context pass — replay against a warm service worker to surface stale cache regressions that fresh runs never reproduce. 5. Tie to the graph — each route becomes a TestWorkflow and each click a TestStep, carrying its screenshot, a pass/fail verdict, and a citation to any rubric guideline it violates; findings queue as pending facts for review. 6. Review and grow — Opus reads the coverage gaps and authors new predetermined paths, so the library grows over time. This page is the goal and workflow overview; the stepped review itself is generated as a TestWorkflow story. Review Page (Mobile) The /review page on mobile viewport. Stacked layout with review panel full width above graph. Touch friendly card actions. Review Split View The /review page with the graph preview and review panel side by side. Diff entries, summary chips, and tab navigation all visible. Settings Page The /settings page with LLM backend selection, API key inputs, model configuration, and export options. Test Suite Reckons.AI test infrastructure: 336+ unit tests (Vitest + jsdom), Playwright E2E with 6 device profiles, visual regression with pixel analysis + DOM overlap + text presence checks, optional Mistral OCR and Claude Vision tiers. All tests run locally without API keys. See also: Start here Unit Tests 336+ tests via Vitest with jsdom environment. Coverage: RDF serialize/import, temporal conflict detection, semantic diff, merge analysis, content safety (28 tests), embedding, mobile auth. Run: npx vitest run. User Story Tests End to end test scenarios that follow real user workflows. Each story imports graphs, navigates pages, takes screenshots at each step, and verifies UI state. Three stories: Dev Sprint Planning, User Docs Import, Cross Graph Alignment. Visual Regression Tests Playwright based visual regression. 5 analysis layers (cheapest first): pixel analysis (solid fill, color anomaly), DOM overlap detection, text presence checks, Mistral OCR (if API key), Claude Vision semantic analysis (if API key). Screenshots saved to tests/visual/screenshots/.

docs.title: How this site is built
docs.excerpt: This documentation site is generated from the graph that describes Reckons.AI — including the parts that are still wrong.
docs.text: How this site is built This site is not written. It is composed — from the same knowledge graph that describes Reckons.AI to itself. This page explains how, and is honest about what does not work yet. It is also the one page here that is genuinely hand written. That is deliberate, and the reason is explained at the bottom. The problem this solves Until recently /docs published one page per entity . Any subject in the documentation graphs carrying a type became its own file, which produced 269 pages sorted alphabetically with no editorial layer. The sidebar was 23,000 pixels tall and held 815 links. Real documentation sat beside internal bookkeeping like "GUIDE.md → Superseded" — a note about this repository's own file migration, published as public documentation. Nothing had gone wrong mechanically. The generator did exactly what it was told. The mistake was in what it was told: "has a type" was standing in for "is a page someone would want to read" , so the graph was deciding the site's information architecture by accident. Three graphs, not one The site is described by three graphs with different jobs. The design graph ( static/website.ttl ) says what the site should be. Eight pages, each declaring which datasets it draws on and — required, not optional — why a reader would open it . A page with no stated purpose is refused at build time, because a page nobody can state the point of is precisely what the 269 already were. It uses standard vocabulary rather than invented terms: schema:WebPage for pages, schema:isBasedOn for the source relation, schema:abstract for purpose, void:Dataset for each source graph, and dcat:Catalog to hold the set together. The status graph ( static/website status.ttl ) says what the site actually is . It is generated by walking the published files and reading each one through the same parser the site uses. Crucially it is derived from the output , never written alongside it — a status graph produced from the same source as the pages would agree with itself by construction and prove nothing. The archive is git, for now. That is a deliberate choice rather than a gap: for text under version control, a parallel journal would duplicate what git already does well. Composition Each page declares its sources, and composition gathers the matching entities into it, grouped by which graph each part came from. One page can draw on several graphs — How it works composes both the architecture and the triples and RDF datasets, and says which section came from which. The safeguard matters more than the feature: composition refuses to run if any entity would be left unclaimed. Reducing 269 pages to 8 is an editorial act, and the difference between curated and we lost 250 pages of content is entirely whether the leftovers are visible. Run npm run docs:consolidate and it reports exactly what every page covers and what nothing covers. Some entities are deliberately excluded , and an exclusion is not the same as an oversight. The markdown migration tracker — those 22 "→ Superseded" entries — is excluded by a rule that carries its reason. An exclusion without a stated reason is refused. Cross links are derived, not written Entities relate to each other in the graph. When consolidation moved them onto shared pages those relationships did not disappear — they became invisible. So the generator reads them back and emits a See also line pointing at whichever page now holds the related entity. Nobody maintains those links. They are recomputed on every build, and they cannot rot into pointing at a page that no longer exists. The site measures itself npm run website:align This compares the design graph against the observed status graph and scores the gap. It keeps four kinds of divergence separate, because they need different responses: Undeclared — published, but the design never asked for it. Wants a decision. Unbuilt — designed, but does not exist. Wants building. Divergent — exists in both, and they disagree. The only unambiguous bug. Aligned — agreement. When this consolidation began the score was 0% : 271 pages the design did not describe and 8 designed pages that did not exist. "The docs are a mess" is true and unactionable; 0% aligned, 271 undeclared is the same statement in a form you can work to zero. What is not built Stating this plainly is a house rule here — a plan written in the present tense is a lie with good manners. The status graph observes files, not rendering. It knows a page exists and what it claims to be. It cannot tell you what a browser actually painted, so a page can appear correct and render broken. The graph records those blind spots explicitly rather than leaving them implied. Section variety. Every composed section renders the same way — a heading and a definition. Cards, callouts and richer layouts are not expressible in the design graph yet. Links into the graph view. A page cannot yet link a reader to the interactive graph its content came from. The deep link does not exist: the app's ?kb= parameter names a local database, not one of these published graphs. Design intent is only partly checked. The graph declares things like disclosure style, and nothing yet verifies the rendered page honours them. Why this page is hand written Every other page here is generated, and editing one directly would be pointless — the next build overwrites it. This page carries no source declaration, which is what marks it hand authored. The generator skips it entirely, the alignment report still counts it, and it is safe to edit by hand or through the CMS. That distinction is the seam the site is being refined through: generated pages are changed by editing the graph; pages like this one are changed by writing. The harder question is what happens when someone edits a generated page to add their own voice. Today the answer is that the next regeneration overwrites it. That is a known limitation with a plan behind it, not a decision anyone is happy with.

docs.title: Reckons.AI v0.1.0
docs.excerpt: The first tagged release: local-first knowledge graphs, multi-provider LLM extraction, 2D/3D graph views, Shelly, a browser extension, an MCP server, cross-KB alignment, and graph-published docs.
docs.text: Reckons.AI v0.1.0 The first tagged release of Reckons.AI, a local first personal knowledge graph that runs entirely in your browser. Here is an honest summary of what shipped. Highlights Local first knowledge graphs — Statements live in IndexedDB (via Dexie); no server is required. Each graph is a portable, versionable store you can export as Turtle at any time. Multi provider LLM extraction with review — Claude, OpenAI, Gemini, Ollama, OpenRouter, Chrome's built in AI, or a fully offline WASM model extract facts from whatever you ingest. Every extracted statement lands in a review workflow (pending, confirmed, refined, rejected, superseded) before it is trusted. 2D and 3D graph views — Explore your knowledge as an interactive force directed graph, with per entity icons, hierarchy layouts, and 3D models for key nodes. Shelly, the in app assistant — A chat companion that can search, explain, and tour your graph, including guided stories with text to speech playback. Browser extension — Capture pages as you browse, accumulate a research session across tabs, and batch ingest with at a glance conflict and reinforcement summaries. MCP server — Query your knowledge graphs from Claude Code, Claude Desktop, or any MCP client: full text search, subgraph traversal, AI grounded reckonings (situation to target to proposal), and git aware alignment checks against a project's own roadmap. Cross KB alignment — Compare and merge entities across two graphs, with embedding based matching and IRI remapping for the parts you accept. Graph published docs — This documentation site is generated from a Reckons.AI graph and published through a Sveltia CMS backed workflow: pages are graph nodes, markdown is a generated by product, and a CI check keeps the two in sync. Under the hood A content safety preamble is injected into every LLM call, backed by a pattern based classifier that filters disallowed content before it ever reaches your graph. BGE small en v1.5 embeddings power semantic search, merge detection, and cross KB entity matching. The product's own roadmap, architecture, and test coverage are documented as queryable TTL knowledge bases rather than scattered markdown files, with a git aware alignment check to catch drift between code and plan. What's next Progressive enrichment pipelines, a VS Code integration, and enterprise access controls are on the roadmap. See the Docs for what has shipped and what is still planned.

docs.title: Reckons.AI v0.2.0
docs.excerpt: The first release since v0.1.0: currents, archive, publishing, a deterministic offline tier — and a run of fixes for features that were green in tests and dead in a browser.
headings: Fixes that matter more than they look
docs.text: Reckons.AI v0.2.0 454 commits since v0.1.0, 157 of them features. This is the honest summary — what shipped, and what is still not true. Highlights Currents — sources you subscribe to, arriving as translucent pod view nodes for review rather than landing silently in the graph. Archive — sweep old facts into a dated archive graph, with a journal that can be rewound. An ingest that mentions an archived entity now offers to restore it instead of quietly minting a duplicate. Graph publishing — WebPage nodes round trip to content/ .md , so this page and the rest of the docs are composed from the graph rather than written beside it. A deterministic offline tier — 19 checks that cost nothing to run: graph invariants, SHACL shapes, CSP origins, claim auditing, safety attestation. They run before every PR and are the reason several of the fixes below were found at all. Multi graph work — cross graph alignment, KB leaps, graph sets, and duplicate detection that can now compare copies rather than only reporting them. Fixes that matter more than they look A theme ran through this release: features that were green in tests and dead in a browser . Repo ingest and site export had never worked from a browser. api.github.com was missing from the Content Security Policy allowlist since the initial release commit, so the browser refused the request before sending it. Both were marked shipped. Also fixed for Tavily, Firecrawl, and the default Reckons provider URL — and a script now checks every fetched origin against the policy, so this class cannot return quietly. Self hosted Indico could never be reached , for the same reason plus missing CORS. The verifier was 6/6 green because it ran in Node, where neither is enforced. The timeline placed undated nodes at their ingestion time , so 93% of the starter graph sat in a wall at "today" and compressed the real events into a tenth of the axis. Undated nodes now get their own labelled lane. Imported events were two hours wrong — Indico renders times in the category's timezone, which the mapper discarded. Safety The ethics preamble is no longer injected into every prompt. It is gated by purpose and locality : anything shared always carries it, remote conversation carries it, and local only or structured output paths do not — the latter because every written statement already passes a deterministic content classifier regardless of what a model was told. The ordering is now tested: a custom persona cannot precede the preamble, and a shared persona served from a local model still carries it. What is still not true The review queue holds 736 proposals and none has ever been ruled on . There is now a metric that says so. Estimates exist on five designs and only two have been scored; both came in under. SHACL validation reports and does not gate — nothing in the app is blocked by a shape yet, and users cannot author shapes for their own graphs. staging had drifted 84 commits behind main ; this release reconciles the pipeline. Seventeen js/file system race findings are open, not the seven an earlier draft of this page claimed — that number came from a partial query and was wrong. Sixteen already existed on main ; this release adds the same pattern in two new scripts. Every one is a check then act on a file ( if (!existsSync(p)) writeFileSync(p, …) ) in build and agent scripts — none of it ships in the app bundle. They are known, unfixed, and deliberately not bundled into this release; the fix is its own branch because it is mechanical and touches twelve files.

docs.title: Reckons.AI v0.2.5
docs.excerpt: The Spaces map, the first half of the Source View, one shared graph canvas, and a local agent tier that does most of the repetitive work on your own hardware.
headings: For developers: the local agent tier
docs.text: Reckons.AI v0.2.5 The first release made the way 0.2.0 said releases should be made: one deliberate set of changes, promoted from dev to staging to main together, with the version number, the build and this page agreeing. Here is what changed, and what is still not true. Highlights The Spaces map. See all of your spaces at once and the links between them, drawn as a tide pool tank. Other spaces load in the background, so the lines appear without a button. This is phase 1; the map as a mode of the shared canvas, and ghost spaces you know about but cannot open, move to 0.2.6. The Source View, first half. A source now keeps its text. Open a source and you see its passages and the statements each one produced. Select a node and you see which sources its facts came from, grouped by source, with a link straight to each. A statement shows the passage it came from as evidence. Long documents are split into recorded pieces, and a cut is never silent. One graph canvas. The review page's preview graph now uses the same canvas as the main view, so a fix to one is a fix to both. The add menu. The + button opens a short menu of what you can add, with a source at the top. Sync to your phone. Send a whole space to the phone's Files app. A sync service's conflict copy can no longer replace or duplicate a space. Calmer labels. A label is shown or hidden, never half visible, and fades between the two. Spoken commands. Commands are recognized through a messy transcript, and the app refuses to guess when it cannot tell. Plain words on screen. The interface says space and graph, not "KB". Safety and correctness Template arguments are quoted for the shell, closing a real injection path. A node id written as a literal can no longer turn into a subject address and break an export. Every space has a stable id, and an import never adopts one already in use. The dependency audit is green again, including a deprecated release that had been pinned. Local machine checks keep their evidence private: only counts leave your machine. For developers: the local agent tier Most of the repetitive work behind this release ran on local models and deterministic scripts rather than a paid cloud model. Thirty six sentences is a report on one session of it. A local panel hands many small judgments to local models and returns only the doubtful ones. agent:watch shows local model activity, the job queue, and a walking turtle; it now starts the queue worker itself. A session gated queue runs local jobs only while you are working, never on an idle machine, and checks GPU heat and memory before each job. A circuit breaker stops a job that keeps failing the same way, and a failing schedule rests instead of looping. Back pressure. A local job whose suggestions nobody has reviewed stops producing more until someone does. Streamed local calls , so a job waiting behind others no longer times out. A merge queue lands green pull requests on dev unattended, and a docs gate blocks a release while any shipped feature lacks a page. Not true yet Big spaces are slow to draw. Measured: at 10,000 statements the first 3D frame takes about 12 seconds; at 100,000 the import takes about two and a half minutes. Rendering is the limit, not the file. The Source View is half built. Keeping folded source chunks inside a space's file needs importer support, which is planned for 0.2.6. Currents moved back to scaffolded. The client that fetches a current's items from n8n is written and tested, but nothing in the app calls it yet, so a current delivers nothing and the pod view has no arrivals to show. The roadmap no longer calls either one functional. Untrusted input hardening is partial. See Treating every input as untrusted.

docs.title: Reckons.AI v0.2.6
docs.excerpt: Follow a fact back to the exact words it came from, a Getting started space that arrives already reviewed, and spaces you can stand inside, with generated pictures, 3D captures and rooms behind the graph.
docs.text: Reckons.AI v0.2.6 This release has one goal and a second one that came along with it. The goal is the evidence chain . A fact in your space now points to the exact words it came from, and that link survives saving, copying and syncing. Facts and their sources used to live in separate places; this release joins them, because a decision is only as good as the evidence you can follow back from it. The second goal is spaces you can stand inside : generated pictures, 3D captures and whole rooms drawn behind your graph. It was built in the same two weeks and is part of the same promotion, so it ships here. It is less finished than the evidence chain, and the last section says where. The evidence chain Open in source. From a fact's evidence, Open in source opens the source, scrolls to the passage, and marks the words the fact was taken from. A fact remembers where its words are. When Reckons.AI reads a source and proposes a fact, the fact records the exact stretch of text it came from. That record survives export, import and sync. A changed source says so. If a source's text changes after a fact was taken from it, the fact's evidence is marked stale ("the source changed" or "the passage moved"). It is never quietly pointed at different words. A space file carries its passages. The passages behind your facts are written into the space's own file, after the facts. Copy that one file to another computer and the evidence comes with it. Sync, Google Drive backups, auto save and export all include them. The groundwork for decisions. A proposal is now defined: two to four options, each citing the facts it rests on, and through them the passages. Nothing in the app makes or shows a proposal yet. Getting started arrives reviewed Sample sources. The Getting started space now comes with seven short sample sources (each says it is a sample) and 48 facts taken from them. Each fact shows its passage, who accepted it and when, including two corrections and two rejections, so the review history is real rather than blank. Three facts left for you. The Review tab opens with three facts waiting for your decision. Review without a download. Opening Review no longer asks you to download a model. Shelly asks first, and only when needed. Shelly asks for permission to use a model when you send a message, not when the tour opens. Honest counts on Review. Items handed to an agent read "waiting for an agent", and the page no longer claims anything was settled without you. Collections. A group of things you made is now called a collection everywhere, and groups made before this release are converted when the space opens. View settings. The panel at the top left of the graph is now View settings, and it holds the space's background controls. A quieter graph. The node that stands for the space itself is shown only at the "all" detail level. Spaces you can stand inside 3D captures on a node. A node can carry a Gaussian splat, a 3D capture drawn as many soft points. You see it in the 3D graph and can turn it in the viewer. Splats hide the nodes, lines and labels behind them. A background for a space. A splat can sit behind the graph, as a backdrop or all around you. Choose its orientation, size, position and opacity, or level its floor, from View settings. Import a scan. Bring in a 3D capture from your device (.ply, .spz or .sog). Large files are stored on your device, never copied into the space's text. Place things in the room. Put a node's splat where you want it inside the background, at the size you want. Three.js scenes. Attach an example from threejs.org to a node, or use one as the background. It runs in a sealed frame and only loads when you ask it to. Two example spaces. Generated assets shows a prompt becoming a picture, a short video and a splat, with the license of every tool that made them. Your room walks through scanning a room, importing it and placing things inside. Prompt, Image, Video, 3D model, Gaussian splat and License are now built in types. Make your own, on your own machine. If you have a capable graphics card, optional commands turn a prompt into a picture, video and splat, or a phone scan of a room into a splat. Every model and tool they use is MIT or Apache 2.0 licensed, runs locally, and is checked by a separate test before its result is used. In the Generated assets space, Shelly can ask that local service for a picture and attach what it actually made. Currents deliver again Currents, which collect items from the web through your own n8n server, reach the app again. Import the Currents Monitor workflow into your n8n server and connect it in Integrations; new items then arrive as facts waiting for your review, and your earlier decisions are kept when an item arrives twice. Without a connected n8n server a current delivers nothing, and its settings now say so instead of claiming it is delivering. Safety and correctness Models pinned to an exact version. The models Reckons.AI ships with are fixed to one exact version, so a change can name the model that made it. Two are not: the Kokoro voice (its loader ignores the version) and any model you type into Settings yourself. You will download each pinned model once more, at its pinned version. Dependency advisories cleared, including in the build tools. A more honest README. It now says plainly which features send data off your device. Older copies of Your room load again after its room file was renamed. For developers CI as a graph. It says which checks can stop a merge to main and which only advise. Who made a change, and why. Agent commits carry Model: and Intent: lines, checked in CI; a pull request into dev may not carry commits that exist only on main. One review queue for the app, the MCP server and the local jobs (there were two). Terminology checks that read only words people see. The UI terms audit finds engineering words on screen by rule, and the term ratchet now counts prose, not code identifiers. Steadier local models. One batch size per device, and a retry when the model server restarts. Visual review. Each test workflow has a page with a diagram and a screenshot per step; each release gets a review space of its own; a local vision model can walk a workflow and report what it sees. A generation bench that says when a newer open model should replace the one in use. A reckoning simulator core. A scene read from the graph, stepped by a physics engine and checked against conditions. It runs from the command line only; nothing in the app uses it yet. Planned, not built These are written into the roadmap, so you can read what is intended. None of them works yet. reckons.space , a registry of shared spaces where every listing names who shared it. Simulated reckonings : proposals tried in a physical scene, scored and replayed. A room from a sentence : a space background made from a text prompt. A Create chapter in Getting started , and stepping into a linked space by zooming into it. An automated review for dev , so agents check and fix every change before a person reviews a release. Not true yet Proposals are a definition only. Building options with their citations, and following a citation to its passage, move to 0.2.7. They had not started when this release closed. Evidence points at text only. A fact can point to a passage of text, not to a page, a box on a page, or a region of an image; that part of the anchor is not built. Your room is a guided example, not a finished feature. Its room is a reconstruction of a computer made scene, not a real scan. A crashing Three.js scene is not fully contained. The sealed frame stops a scene from reaching your data, but a scene that crashes the browser's graphics driver can still take the page down. Making your own assets is demanding. It was measured on one Linux machine with one NVIDIA RTX 3090. Picture, video and splat took about 15 to 55 seconds each there; a room scan took about 20 minutes. docs.title: Reckons.AI v0.2.7
docs.excerpt: The agents release: a This Device page that shows your local AI helpers at work, review links that open the right space, questions settled from earlier decisions before they reach you, and a local stand-in that keeps working when cloud usage runs out.
headings: A local stand-in when cloud usage runs out
docs.text: Reckons.AI v0.2.7 This is the agents release . Reckons.AI is built with the help of AI agents: some run in the cloud, and some run on the computer in front of you, on models you download once and own. This release is about those agents. It gives you a place to watch them, makes their work quicker to review, and lets them keep going when cloud usage runs out. Be clear about one thing first: most of what is in here serves the people building Reckons.AI and anyone who runs its agents themselves. If you use the app to keep your own knowledge, the change you will notice is the new This Device page in Settings. Nothing about how you keep and review your knowledge has changed. This Device A new page in Settings. Settings → This Device shows the computer you are on, the browser you are using, and what is installed: local AI models, connected tools, the browser extension and your app integrations. An integration shows as "configured", never "working", because the page cannot prove it works. Watch the agents. A Start button runs the agent watch from the page. A pinned row shows what matters at a glance (the queue, the local model server, what is running, failures in the last hour, the graphics card) and the detail folds away below it. It used to live only in a terminal window that kept scrolling away. Where it works. The watch reads the computer that runs the models, so it needs the development server on that computer. Opened anywhere else, the page still shows your browser and explains how to start the watch where the models are. Reviewing agent work is quicker Links that land in the right place. When an agent asks you to review its work, the link now opens the right space and the right batch, grouped by the run that produced it. If the app has lost permission to your folder, you get one Reconnect button instead of an empty page. Questions are settled before they reach you. When an agent has a question, it first looks for a decision you already recorded. It may answer only by quoting that decision word for word. A check refuses any quote that is not really there, and a second model has to agree the quote settles the question. Only what is still open comes to you. A cleaner queue. A check now finds damaged lines in the review queue, and agents that add to the queue take turns instead of writing over each other. On the day it ran, 15 damaged lines and 110 duplicates were cleared out. A local stand in when cloud usage runs out The local deputy. When the cloud model's usage runs out, a local model can carry on in the same coding tool, with the same rules. It cannot push code or merge anything, and it uses no cloud account. Everything it does is a proposal that the next cloud session reviews. It is slower and less capable than the cloud model, and it is told to say so rather than guess. It remembers carefully. What the stand in learned in one session is kept aside for review, not merged into its memory automatically, and the next session is told it is waiting. It can work on another project. The stand in and the Reckons.AI tools can now work inside a different repository, such as a website managed with Reckons.AI, and follow that project's own rules. The first person to run it in a new folder has to approve that folder once. Measured, not assumed. Before trusting a local model to check other agents' work, we gave it six cases with known answers, five times each. It got 26 of 30 right. Most of its misses were stopping to ask when it should have carried on, which is the safer kind of mistake, but it is still a mistake. Steps that cannot be skipped Agents work fast, and fast work skips steps. This release starts moving the rules that matter from written instructions into checks that run by themselves: a job must say how you will know it is done before an agent can be handed it, and checks run when work is committed and pushed. This is in progress. The brief check confirms the done test is there, not that it is a good one, and most rules are still written down. Moved to v0.2.8 v0.2.7 was first planned as the "reach" release: serving Reckons.AI from your own computer to your other devices. None of that had started, so it moves to v0.2.8 , together with the canvas and analysis work that was moved here from v0.2.6. Moved because it was not started, not because it was dropped.

docs.title: Reckons.AI Graph Review — Goal & Workflow
docs.excerpt: The Reckons.AI Graph Review is an offline, exhaustive audit of the whole app treated as a graph: every button is clicked, every screen is visually checked, and every finding is tied back to the graph for human review.
docs.text: Reckons.AI Graph Review — Goal & Workflow The Reckons.AI Graph Review is an offline, exhaustive audit of the whole app treated as a graph: every button is clicked, every screen is visually checked, and every finding is tied back to the graph for human review. It runs locally and Opus reviewed — no cloud dependency — and scores against the Web/Mobile UI UX rubric. The goal Catch the failures a "click everything, flag crashes" pass misses — silent no ops (a control that fires, throws nothing, and does nothing) and stale cache regressions — while producing a reviewable, graph native record rather than a throwaway log. Workflow overview 1. Enumerate — collect every interactive element on every route (buttons, tabs, leap badges, sheets). 2. Act and assert a delta — click each, then check that something observable actually changed (URL, node count, graph id, open panels, title, visible text). This is what catches silent no ops. 3. Visual check — pixel, DOM overlap and touch target checks run locally; a local VLM scores each screenshot against the rubric. 4. Persistent context pass — replay against a warm service worker to surface stale cache regressions that fresh runs never reproduce. 5. Tie to the graph — each route becomes a TestWorkflow and each click a TestStep, carrying its screenshot, a pass/fail verdict, and a citation to any rubric guideline it violates; findings queue as pending facts for review. 6. Review and grow — Opus reads the coverage gaps and authors new predetermined paths, so the library grows over time. This page is the goal and workflow overview; the stepped review itself is generated as a TestWorkflow story.

docs.text: Test workflows A test workflow is one whole task a person does in Reckons.AI, written down as numbered steps and then run, step by step, by an automated test in a real browser. Each workflow page shows the steps as a diagram, says in plain words what happens at each step, shows a screenshot of the real app with a box drawn round the control being checked, and states the one thing the test checks at that step. Why a page for each A passing test only says "nothing broke". A workflow page lets a person who has never opened the app see what the test actually does, in the order they would do it, and judge for themselves whether the check at each step is a meaningful one. How to read a workflow page 1. The diagram is drawn from the step list itself, so it always matches what the test runs. 2. Each step has the words for what happens, where it happens, the screenshot, then What the test checks . 3. The pink box in a screenshot marks the control or area that step is about. What is honest about this Screenshots are taken on synthetic example data, never on anyone's real notes. A step whose screenshot has not been captured yet says so instead of showing a stand in picture. The test confirms the app responds at every step; it does not judge how good the extracted claims or a reckoning's proposal are, which are measured separately. Each workflow page says which parts are scripted stand ins for a model.

docs.title: Local VLM workflow streams
docs.excerpt: Each stream uses fresh browser storage, synthetic UI inputs and an explicit loopback app origin.
docs.text: Local VLM workflow streams Each stream uses fresh browser storage, synthetic UI inputs and an explicit loopback app origin. Network requests are limited to same origin GET/HEAD; service workers, websocket connections, popups and downloads are unavailable. Real external integrations are outside this harness. Artifacts are private under XDG STATE HOME/reckons/visual streams (default ~/.local/state), with ordered screenshots and hashes, configuration, raw model responses, validated actions, browser errors and assertion results. Run provenance records the checkout commit and dirty flag; it does not attest which build the supplied preview serves. Run several independent visual analysis streams against a local branch preview. A scripted stream follows configured goto, click and fill steps. An exploratory stream asks a local vision model to choose a visible control, type, scroll, press a key or finish. Each checkpoint runs separate configured analysis lenses, such as layout, readability and progress, with the preceding screenshot available for comparison. Streams run sequentially to avoid competing for GPU memory. The JSON version is 1. Each stream has a unique id, mode, goal, startPath and nonempty lenses (id and question). Optional model, viewport, mobile, timeoutMs and maxSteps bound a run. Scripted streams require steps; exploratory streams use screenshot grounded actions instead. Optional assertions check an exact path or a visible unique selector, with optional contained text. Selector assertions check rendered browser state; they cannot prove a database write unless the workflow exposes that outcome. Why it is this way Honest Note A verified goal means configured browser assertions passed, not that the VLM's visual judgment is correct. Goal driven exploration stops when all assertions hold. Without assertions, a model finish is unverified. Step exhaustion, malformed output, deadline and browser failures are incomplete/error results. Visual issues and uncertainty become proposals in the main workspace review queue. CLI exit 2 means failed/incomplete execution, exit 1 means visual proposals need review, exit 0 means the run completed; read each stream status. No cloud fallback and no product edits. This is a local tool, not an autonomous CI approval gate. Detail Command Start a preview, then OLLAMA BASE URL=http://localhost:11434 npm run visual:streams base=http://localhost:4173. Use list to validate and list examples, streams=find review to select, model=qwen2.5vl:7b to override models, and config=path/to/streams.json for custom workflows. scripts/visual streams/examples.json is the executable contract example. docs.text: Make pictures, clips and 3D splats on your own machine, and see them in a space Write a prompt, and three local models turn it into a picture, then a short clip and a Gaussian splat (a 3D object drawn as many small soft blobs of color) made from that picture. You can turn a splat and look at it from any side. The results open as their own space, where each one sits on its own node, linked to what it was made from, and one splat can become the background of the space. Made on one machine, with no cloud service Step Tool Model License What it made Picture from a prompt stable diffusion.cpp Z Image Turbo MIT and Apache 2.0 a 768×768 picture Clip from the picture stable diffusion.cpp Wan2.2 TI2V 5B MIT and Apache 2.0 a 3 second, 49 frame clip Splat from the picture TripoSplat TripoSplat MIT 32,768 or 65,536 Gaussians All three run on your own computer. The command is npm run gen:assets , which reads made up prompts from scripts/content/gen briefs.json . Each result gets a receipt beside it that names the tool, every model file with its fingerprint (a SHA 256 hash) and license, the prompt, the seed, how long it took, and whether the result passed its check. Tools and model files live outside the project folder; scripts/content/gen setup.sh downloads them. A result is accepted by a check, not by the tool A model can write a grey square, a clip in which nothing moves, or a splat full of broken numbers, and still report success. So every result is checked by code that knows nothing about the model. The picture must not be flat. The clip must play, and how much it moves is measured. The splat must have the expected number of blobs, real numbers, a real size and visible blobs. On the first run the splat check found a fault in TripoSplat's own file writer: thousands of blobs were saved with an infinite opacity. The pipeline now repairs those values and records how many it repaired. A generated splat is invented TripoSplat guesses the far side of an object from one picture. A splat made this way is decoration, not a record of anything real, and the space says so. A splat rebuilt from many real photographs is a different thing and is not part of this workflow. The steps of this workflow, drawn from the same list the test runs. How these screenshots were made What they show. The pictures, clips and splats are the committed results of one run of npm run gen:assets on one machine with an NVIDIA RTX 3090 graphics card, on 2026 10 14. Every prompt is made up for this example. What is not run here. The browser test cannot run the models, because the machines that run the tests have no graphics card. For each result it checks that the file the app shows is byte for byte the one its receipt describes, that its check accepted it when it was made, and that the app shows it. Whether the models still produce good results is checked only when someone runs npm run gen:assets again. The steps 1. Open the Generated assets example as its own space Under example data on the About page (or from the welcome page), choose Generated assets. It opens as a new space of its own and shows its graph, so trying it never mixes into the space you were working in. Opening it again refreshes that same space rather than making a second one. Where: the About page ( /about ). The pink box marks the Generated assets card under example data. What the test checks. The card offers to open the example as a space; choosing it lands on the graph of the new space, and the Spaces tab then shows Generated assets as the current space. 2. See the pipeline in the graph Each result is a node, linked to what it was made from: a prompt to its picture, and the picture to its clip and its splat. Each node lists what its receipt recorded (the model, the seed, how long it took and when) under metadata in its details, not as extra nodes, and its license is a node of its own (MIT or Apache 2.0) that it links to. Turn on preview all to see every result on its node. A node with a splat is drawn inside its splat, which turns slowly. Where: the graph ( / ). The pink box marks the graph, where each prompt links to its picture and the picture links to its clip and its splat. What the test checks. With previews on, at least three results show on their nodes (which ones are in view depends on where the layout puts them), and the 3D graph reports both node splats loaded and none failed. 3. The picture, made from a prompt Z Image Turbo, run by stable diffusion.cpp, turned the prompt into a 768×768 picture in eight steps. Find the picture's node (searching for its name works when it is out of view) and choose its preview to see it large. This picture is the starting point for the next two steps. Where: the graph ( / ). The pink box marks the enlarged picture. What the test checks. The picture the app shows is byte for byte the file its receipt describes (same SHA 256), its check accepted it, its models are MIT or Apache 2.0 licensed, and it opens large at 768 pixels wide. 4. The clip, made from the picture Wan2.2 TI2V 5B, also run by stable diffusion.cpp, started from the picture and a second prompt describing the motion, and made a 49 frame clip. The check measures how much the last frame differs from the first, because a video model can return a clip in which almost nothing moves. When that happens the receipt says so rather than calling the clip fine. Where: the graph ( / ). The pink box marks the clip, paused part way through. What the test checks. The clip the app shows matches its receipt, its check accepted it, and it loads in the viewer at 512 pixels wide. The screenshot shows a frame from the middle of the clip. 5. The splat, made from the picture TripoSplat turned the same picture into 32,768 Gaussians, writing a PLY file of about 2 MB. The first prompt asked for a flat carving seen from above, and TripoSplat made it as flat as a coin; asking for a three quarter view with a domed shell gave it real depth. Choose the splat on its node to turn it and look at it from any side. Everything it shows on the far side of the turtle was guessed from one picture. Where: the graph ( / ). The pink box marks the splat viewer, which turns the splat slowly and can be dragged. What the test checks. The splat the app shows matches its receipt and its check accepted it, and the viewer reports that it has loaded. The renderer is Gaussian Splat Lite, which the app loads only when a splat is on screen. 6. Set a splat as the background of the space Open the lighthouse island splat and choose Set as background. The island is then drawn large behind the graph, sized to the graph and turning very slowly, and it never gets in the way of choosing a node. The choice is saved with the space, so it travels with an export. Clear background removes it. Where: the graph ( / ). The pink box marks the graph with the lighthouse island splat drawn behind it. What the test checks. The island splat matches its receipt. After Set as background the same control offers Clear background, which shows the setting was saved to the space, and the 3D graph reports three splats loaded and none failed: the two on their nodes and the island. Where the island sits and how it looks is shown by the screenshot, not measured by the test. This workflow is run by tests/e2e/workflow generated assets.test.ts , which reads the steps above from the same list.

docs.text: Add a source, review it, see it in a space, ask for a reckoning The path the README describes, start to finish: put a short note into Reckons.AI, settle the claims it proposes, find them in your space, and ask for a reckoning that works from what you settled. It is the whole point of the product in five steps, and a browser test runs it on every change. The steps of this workflow, drawn from the same list the test runs. How these screenshots were made What they show. Every step is run on the Getting started sample that a first time visitor opens, in which two people, Alex and Jordan, plan a camping weekend. Everything in it is invented, so the claims, counts and names in the pictures are sample content and not anyone's real notes. What is scripted. The test uses no language model. When it adds its own note in step 1, a stand in reader returns placeholder claims, so the claims you see waiting in steps 2 and 3 are the ones Getting started already holds. In step 5 the reckoning is a fixed reply, written in advance to read like a real one. So the pictures show what each screen looks like and that it responds. They do not show how good a real model's claims or proposal would be, which is measured separately. The steps 1. Add a source Open the Add tab, give the note a title, type or paste in a few sentences and press Extract facts. Reckons.AI reads the text and proposes claims from it. Nothing is accepted yet: every claim arrives waiting for your decision. Where: the Add tab ( /ingest ). The pink box marks the Extract facts button, under the note's title and text. What the test checks. The Extract facts button is enabled once a title and text are entered, and pressing it takes the person off the Add tab when reading finishes. The test's stand in reader returns placeholder claims at this point. 2. Review the proposed claims Open Review. Each claim waiting for a decision is a card. It names where the claim came from, shows the passage it was taken from, and offers accept, refine and reject. AI can misread what it reads, so this is where you check what it proposed against the original text. Where: the Review tab ( /review ). The pink box marks one claim card: the claim, the passage it was taken from, and its accept, refine and reject buttons. What the test checks. At least one claim is waiting on the Review tab, shown as a card with accept, refine and reject buttons. 3. Confirm the claims that are right Press accept on each claim that matches its source. You can also refine a claim or reject it. Only claims you confirm become part of the space; anything left waiting stays out. Where: the Review tab ( /review ). The pink box marks the accept button on the first claim card. What the test checks. Pressing accept settles the claims one by one until none of them is left waiting for a decision. 4. See the claims in your space Open Spaces. The claims you confirmed are now facts in your space, the collection of connected knowledge that everything you add feeds. The one you are working in is marked current, and its card says how many facts it holds. Where: the Spaces tab ( /kb ). The pink box marks the card marked current, which shows its name and how many facts it holds. What the test checks. The Spaces tab shows the current one with more facts than it held before the claims were confirmed. 5. Ask for a reckoning Describe the situation you are in, say what you want to reach, and ask for a reckoning. It reads the facts in your space and proposes options and a recommendation, which you then weigh yourself. It is a proposal to evaluate, not an answer to trust. Where: the Reckon tab ( /reckoning ). The pink box marks the proposal card, which says how many facts it is based on. What the test checks. The request is accepted and a proposal card comes back saying how many facts it is based on. The reply in this run is scripted, written to read like a real reckoning about the Getting started notes; the test does not judge a real model's wording, which is measured separately. This workflow is run by tests/e2e/workflow readme path.test.ts , which reads the steps above from the same list.

docs.title: Privacy and Network Boundaries
docs.excerpt: Local storage does not mean zero network activity.
docs.text: Privacy and Network Boundaries Local storage does not mean zero network activity. The core app stores graphs and settings in the browser and has no required Reckons.AI account or general app backend. Cloud AI requests send task content and relevant facts to the configured provider, with credentials used to authenticate requests. URL ingestion uses Jina Reader or a configured scraper; remote OCR sends documents or images to its provider. Enabled Drive or n8n sync can transfer graphs in the background. Sharing, publishing, and connected MCP clients also cross the local storage boundary. On device inference avoids sending inference inputs to a remote model, but model assets must first be downloaded or sideloaded, and an Ollama endpoint can itself be remote. Prefer local routing can fall back to the configured provider; it is not an offline lock. The hosted site permits Cloudflare Web Analytics for visit and performance measurement: src/app.html allows its script and reporting origin, while injection and route coverage depend on hosting configuration. A static build alone does not prove that analytics excludes app routes or that third parties receive no data. This documentation does not claim a deployment wide network or telemetry audit. Review your provider, per task, sync and integration settings before using sensitive material.

docs.title: The Set
docs.excerpt: A set is a named group of things, and it is made of ordinary statements just like everything else here.
docs.text: The Set A set is a named group of things, and it is made of ordinary statements just like everything else here. Where a triple says something about ONE thing, a set says something about SEVERAL at once that these three vendors are the shortlist, that these five steps are the recipe. It has a name, a description and facts of its own, so you can say things about the group without saying them about each member.

docs.title: How groups are found when you add something
docs.excerpt: When you add a note or a document, Reckons.AI looks for groups in what it just read, as a separate step after it has worked out the individual facts.
docs.text: How groups are found when you add something When you add a note or a document, Reckons.AI looks for groups in what it just read, as a separate step after it has worked out the individual facts. It only proposes a group where your text already put several things under one heading it does not guess that a list is a group, and it never adds one on its own. Every proposal waits for you in Review, and it says why it grouped what it did. Why it is this way Note It says what it REFUSED as well as what it found. A grouping step that only reports its successes looks cleverer than it is in the benchmark that informed this, the two models with a perfect record for not over grouping achieved it by never grouping anything at all.

docs.title: A set can keep your own word for membership
docs.excerpt: Most groupings already exist in your notes under a word you chose -- a project 'includes' these tasks, a menu 'offers' these dishes.
docs.text: A set can keep your own word for membership Most groupings already exist in your notes under a word you chose a project 'includes' these tasks, a menu 'offers' these dishes. Reckons.AI can mark that thing as a set without rewriting any of it, by recording which of your words carries the membership. Your vocabulary is kept; nothing is duplicated; and the group becomes something you can name, describe and view as a whole. What we found Example 'Project Ash includes design, build, handover' stays exactly as written. One extra fact says Project Ash is a set, and another says that 'includes' is what its membership is carried by.

docs.title: Order belongs to the membership, not to the member
docs.excerpt: Some sets are sequences -- the steps of a recipe, the stages of a process.
docs.text: Order belongs to the membership, not to the member Some sets are sequences the steps of a recipe, the stages of a process. When order matters, the position is recorded against the PAIR of set and member rather than against the member, because the same thing can be third in one sequence and first in another. A step is not inherently step four; it is step four of this particular process. Why it is this way Note Most sets are not sequences and pay nothing for this. Ordering a set costs about four times as much storage per member as leaving it unordered, so it is worth applying only where the sequence actually carries meaning.

docs.title: Membership overlaps -- it does not file things away
docs.excerpt: A thing can belong to as many sets as it really belongs to.
docs.text: Membership overlaps it does not file things away A thing can belong to as many sets as it really belongs to. A vendor can be on the shortlist AND already deployed; a person can be in the project team AND the football team. This is the difference between a set and a folder: a folder makes you choose one home for a thing, and choosing wrongly hides it. Where two sets share members, that shared part is itself worth looking at Reckons.AI works it out rather than asking you to maintain a list of related things by hand. Why it is this way Note This turned out to be the hard part for automatic grouping. In a benchmark of four local AI models across five runs each, not one ever put a single thing into two sets every model filed each thing in exactly one place. It is the main reason grouping here does not rely on a model.

docs.title: What a set says that triples cannot
docs.excerpt: Triples alone cannot tell the difference between a fact about a GROUP and the same fact about each of its members.
docs.text: What a set says that triples cannot Triples alone cannot tell the difference between a fact about a GROUP and the same fact about each of its members. 'The team weighs 800 kilos' and 'each person on the team weighs 800 kilos' come out identical if the only thing you can describe is one member at a time. Giving the group its own name and its own facts separates them. That is the one thing a set genuinely adds, and it is why sets are part of the substrate rather than a way of laying out a page. What we found Example A set called 'DAM shortlist' can carry 'decided on 2026 08 14' and 'three of eleven considered' facts about the shortlist, true of no single vendor in it.

docs.title: Software engineering
docs.excerpt: Reckons.AI is built with Reckons.AI, and that is the honest reason this use case is the most detailed one here: it is the only one we have run for a year.
headings: Coding agents that start already knowing
Documentation that cannot quietly go stale
docs.text: Software engineering Reckons.AI is built with Reckons.AI, and that is the honest reason this use case is the most detailed one here: it is the only one we have run for a year. A codebase accumulates decisions faster than anything else you own — why a boundary exists, what a change would break, which claim a test actually pins — and almost none of it survives in the code. It ends up in commit messages nobody re reads, in chat histories that expire, and in the heads of whoever was there. The graph is where those decisions are kept as facts you can query, and the pages you are reading are generated from it.

docs.title: Why a graph, and not a notepad
docs.excerpt: Take one sentence from a real working note: Vantage Suite was dropped at this stage on file format grounds.
docs.text: Why a graph, and not a notepad Take one sentence from a real working note: Vantage Suite was dropped at this stage on file format grounds. A notepad keeps the sentence. Reckons.AI keeps the fact underneath it. The difference does not show at ten notes and decides everything at a thousand, because the question you will eventually ask is not what did I write, it is what did we drop, and why. The same sentence, two destinations. The divergence is invisible until you ask a question that spans more notes than you can re read. Why it is this way Principle The step in the middle is where you stay in charge. Extraction proposes; nothing enters your graph until you accept it. That is the same review queue the machine's own findings go through, which is why a wrong reading is a thing you correct in one place rather than a wrong sentence you have to remember not to trust. This is not an argument against note taking, and reading it that way loses what it says. Capture should be as close to frictionless as it can be — talking at your phone should be enough. The claim is about what happens AFTER capture: a pile of prose is a pile you must re read, and re reading does not scale. Structure is the price of being able to ask the pile a question later. Honest Note The product has not been showing this. A careful first time reader read Reckons.AI as generic storyboarding and note taking, twice, on 2026 09 06 and again on 2026 09 08 after further exposure. That is a finding about this product rather than about the reader: if the condensation is not visible on the way in, what is left genuinely does look like a notes app that asks you to do extra work in the middle. This page exists because the argument was being asserted and never shown. What we found Measured HOW STANDARD IS IT, HONESTLY? Counted across every graph in this repository on 2026 09 08: 6,895 uses of standard vocabulary predicates against 10,286 local urn: ones — SKOS alone accounts for 1,847, with dcterms at 317 and PROV at 234. So the SKELETON is standard and the DOMAIN VOCABULARY largely is not. That split is the honest version of the claim: two graphs can be aligned on their structure the day they meet, because both say skos:broader and rdfs:label; aligning what their predicates MEAN is the work, and it is exactly the work the fifty one rival names above describe. Cross Graph Alignment exists here and does the first part; the second is still being built. The divergence is measured, NOT ASSERTED. On 2026 09 08 six local models each read the same short document five times. Twelve relations came back under FIFTY ONE different names. The single relation dropped because was written eleven ways in thirty readings: was eliminated, was dropped on, dropped from shortlist, excluded from shortlist due to, was dropped due to, was dropped from shortlist due to, was eliminated from shortlist, was excluded from shortlist because of, was dropped from shortlist reason, was dropped from shortlist reason for, and dropped from shortlist due to. is a drew eleven names, lacks eight, concern and role five each. Example And the second thing a notepad cannot do: tell you that two of your notes disagree. When a new source arrives, Reckons.AI does not show you everything it found — it shows you what changed: facts that are new, facts that contradict something you already confirmed, and near duplicates of things you already have. The contradictions are the valuable part. A second source disagreeing with the first is the exact moment you want to be interrupted, and it is precisely the moment a folder of documents stays silent — both notes are still there, both still look true, and nothing in the pile knows they cannot both be. And the third thing, which is the one you cannot get to by writing more carefully: a notepad has no COMMON LANGUAGE with anyone else's notepad. Reckons.AI writes its structure in SKOS and the other standard vocabularies — rdf:type, rdfs:label, skos:broader, skos:definition, dcterms and PROV — which are not our invention and not our property. So somebody else's graph, built for their own reasons in their own words, still has a shape yours can be laid against: same relations for is a kind of, same relations for what this is called, same way of saying where a claim came from. Two piles of prose have nothing to lay against each other at all. Doing that by hand is miserable, and that is the actual argument for the machine. Writing SKOS carefully as you take notes is not something anyone will keep up, which is why extraction proposes the structure and you only judge it. The tedious, standardised half is the half a machine is good at; the half that needs you is deciding whether the claim is true. Get that division backwards — a person doing the formatting and a model doing the deciding — and you have the worst of both. That comparison is only possible because the unit is a claim rather than a paragraph. Two paragraphs about the same vendor do not contradict each other in any way a machine can see; two triples with the same subject and predicate and different objects do, exactly and cheaply. It is the same property that makes the fifty one names above a solvable problem instead of a search problem. What that costs you, CONCRETELY. Those eleven phrasings are what a year of your own notes looks like, because you do not phrase things the same way twice either. In a notepad they are eleven unrelated strings: searching dropped finds four of them, and nothing tells you the other seven exist. In a graph they are one relation carrying ten alternative labels, so the question is answered once and completely. That is the whole of the efficiency claim, and it is why the extra step in the middle is not busywork. Example In 'Vantage Suite was dropped on file format grounds': vantage suite = subject, dropped because = predicate, file format = object. Related Watch the diff, not the fact list

The contradictions are the valuable part — a second source disagreeing with the first is the exact signal the review queue exists for, and it should be settled rather than silently overwritten.

headings: Write it the way you would have anyway
docs.text: Keeping everyday notes Scaffolded — the structure exists, but it is incomplete. Expect gaps. You want to write things down the way you always have — loosely, in your own words, without deciding up front what any of it means. The difference here is what happens next: the note is kept as you wrote it AND read for the separate claims inside it, so later you can ask what you actually know rather than search for a paragraph you half remember. The note survives as written; the claims inside it become separately reviewable. The dotted line is the promise that structuring never costs you the original.

docs.title: The paths are not separate products
docs.excerpt: One person moves between all five as their work changes: research until there is enough to decide, reckon to decide it, compare against a colleague who disagreed, then turn the settled result into a story for whoever comes next.
docs.text: The paths are not separate products One person moves between all five as their work changes: research until there is enough to decide, reckon to decide it, compare against a colleague who disagreed, then turn the settled result into a story for whoever comes next. The graph is the same object throughout — that continuity is the point of the whole app. Why it is this way Principle The sharing direction is researcher > LEARNER (the person the story is shared with), and it only works if review happened. A story built on unreviewed facts teaches someone a graph nobody checked, with all the authority of a finished artifact and none of the verification. Review is not admin overhead in front of the fun part; it is what makes the sharing honest.

docs.text: Using reckoning to decide something Functional — built and working, with rough edges still being smoothed. You have a graph and a decision. Reckoning reads the graph as SITUATION (where things stand), TARGET (where you want to be) and PROPOSAL (what would close the gap) — grounded in the facts you confirmed, not in what a model recalls about the subject. A reckoning cites the facts it used, so any part of it can be followed back and disagreed with.

docs.excerpt: The comparison with Palantir and Databricks is true, and it is not the product.
headings: Accessibility is the feature, not a compliance chore
Teaching the shift from documents to things
docs.text: It is a notes app, and the extra step is the point The comparison with Palantir and Databricks is true, and it is not the product. Reckons.AI is a personal assistant that takes notes. You capture something by typing it, pasting it, or saying it out loud, and it works out the claims inside and asks you to confirm them. Everything else here, from the open standards to the 3D graph to the agent tooling, is what that extra step buys. None of it is the reason to open the app.

docs.title: Democratise it
docs.excerpt: Governments and banks pay millions a year to represent what they know as triples, because knowing what you know, and where each piece of it came from, turns out to be the thing that lets an organisation act.
docs.text: Democratise it Governments and banks pay millions a year to represent what they know as triples, because knowing what you know, and where each piece of it came from, turns out to be the thing that lets an organisation act. That capability has no business being restricted to organisations with a procurement department. The standards are open, the models run locally, and the storage is a file. Reckons.AI is what is left when you remove the invoice. Why it is this way Principle An unverifiable claim, made by the party it benefits, is not evidence. Strip the branding and the machinery underneath is the same: typed things, typed relationships between them, and a store you can reason over. That is an RDF graph, whatever the brochure calls it. Every figure below was checked on 16 September 2026 and carries its source. The technology is the same on both routes. What differs is who is allowed to reach it.

docs.title: Why not just use an open-source tool?
docs.excerpt: Because the field splits this problem in two and solves each half separately.
headings: A graph you can actually look at
Where the open-source field beats us
docs.text: Why not just use an open source tool? Because the field splits this problem in two and solves each half separately. The personal knowledge tools, including Logseq, SiYuan, Trilium and Obsidian, have spent years making capture effortless, but their graph is a backlink graph over documents: the nodes are pages and the links mean nothing in particular, so you cannot ask the graph a question. The RDF tools model meaning properly and assume you arrive with an ontology, a server and a SPARQL endpoint. Reckons.AI is the part in between, and it stands on the notes side of it. You capture the way you would anywhere else, and what comes back is a graph.

docs.text: What the subscription actually buys Not the triples, which are a W3C standard anyone may use. The invoice buys scale, support, governance and somebody to sue. Those are real goods, worth real money to an organisation that needs them. What they are not is a prerequisite for representing what you know as typed, sourced, answerable facts.

docs.title: Why Reckons.AI
docs.excerpt: Enterprise technology without the subscription.
docs.text: Why Reckons.AI Enterprise technology without the subscription. The largest data platforms on earth have converged on one way of representing meaning: the RDF triple, which is just a sentence with three parts. They sell it to governments and banks for six and seven figures a year. Reckons.AI is that same representation, running on your own machine, under an MIT licence, with no account and no invoice.
